rv.q: That it works as well as it does at times is no mean feat, but, lacking a strong raison d’etre besides giving us a nibble of history and a few baubles of mirth, this interloper’s reign looks set to be short-lived and immemorable.

There are a few good gags but mostly the script limps along, bedevilled by flaccid, smutty jokes that surely wouldn’t make it past the first draft of a self-respecting Restoration comedy, while the plot meanders in and out of focus.

The trump card is Al Murray’s randy, merry monarch - imagine the late Leslie Phillips in a spaniel wig with the vowels of our current King Charles: the crown is a crine as the opposite of a smile is a frine.
As far as the rest of the show goes, the publicity material should say “undercooked”, “patchy” and “heaven knows how they hooked Carrie Hope Fletcher”.
Nye spends so much time screaming ’this actually happened’, with facts and titbits, that fundamentals such as characterisation, motivation, clarity and structure get left behind.
I'm afraid this is a show on which Murray's pub landlord should really be calling time.
This is the funniest moment in a woefully tedious evening.
It manages to be at once simple-minded and confusing, skimpy and flabby – a show stuffed with stars but devoid of star quality.
But he’d better be ready – because this one is a tedious and almost totally insipid mess.
Murray’s King Charles is a stunning display by someone who knows how to play with an audience with a great running gag with inferences to England's Dutch enemy.
The Crown Jewels is part panto, part stand-up and the actual plot of the play is thin, dull and slows the pace right down.
More of that inventiveness is needed to turn this fitfully funny historical curio into a crowning achievement.
There’s barely enough material here for a sketch show let alone a full-length play and the script is padded out with meandering scenes and underdeveloped characters.

It’s colourful to look at; the costumes are good, as is the revolving set that conveys the different locations...The final number proclaiming that Britons are best and all other nations are inferior is surely meant to be ironic but, like much on offer here, it’s too bland to land a punch.
After two hours of Simon Nye’s pedestrian telling of the tale as a comedy, you have your answer.

Ten years after the Stuart dynasty has been returned to the throne and with Ireland reduced to little more than a serf state, Colonel Blood (Aiden McArdle) attempts a daring heist to strike a blow against the English oppressor.
In all honesty, even as a keen fan of The Windsors onstage I found much of it – mostly the chat between the conspirators – woefully flat.
Overall, there’s just about enough here for an amusing evening out but it might be a bit much for those only mildly interested in the true story.

The rest of this ‘heist’ is an excruciatingly unfunny exercise in making the audience feel slightly less resentful at having paid money for an experience akin to being tortured in the Tower of London.

cn.t: Despite a starry cast including Al Murray and Mel Giedroyc, critics find this heist comedy about Colonel Blood's 1671 theft attempt mostly lifeless and unfunny, with Simon Nye's script squandering an intriguing true story on limp jokes and pedestrian storytelling.
